questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() for Strings in Java?
questions.title: == vs .equals() for Strings in Java
questions.direct_answer: `==` compares **object identity** — it checks whether two variables point to the exact same memory address. `.equals()` compares **content** — it checks whether two Strings contain the same sequence of characters. For String comparison, always use `.equals()`; `==` produces unpredictable results depending on how each String was created.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know that == checks address and .equals() checks content, and can explain why == sometimes works by accident (String pool) but is unreliable.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying == works fine for Strings because it works during simple tests with literals. It fails the moment a String comes from user input, a file read, a REST response, or new String().
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive comparison, and Objects.equals(s1, s2) as the null-safe way to compare without a NullPointerException.

sections.title: Same Text, Different Objects — Why == Lies About Strings
sections.content:
At the plainest level: `==` checks whether two variables point to the **same object**, while `.equals()` checks whether two Strings hold the **same characters**. For comparing what a String actually says, you always want `.equals()`.

`==` was built for primitives like `int`, where there are no objects — it just compares raw values. For objects it is different: a String variable does not hold the text, it holds a **reference** (a memory address). So `==` compares addresses, and two separate objects holding `"hello"` live at different addresses.

`.equals()` works differently. `String` overrides it to walk both strings character by character and return `true` whenever the contents match — no matter how or where each String was created.

The nuance that fools everyone is the **String pool**. Identical literals in your source share one pooled object, so `==` accidentally returns `true` and the bug stays hidden during quick tests.

The gotcha lands the moment a String comes from outside your code — `scanner.nextLine()`, a REST response, a database row, or `new String("hello")`. Each is a fresh heap object, so `==` returns `false` even when the text matches perfectly.

```java
String input = scanner.nextLine(); // user types: hello
if (input == "hello")              // always false — input is a new object
    System.out.println("Match");
```

The fix is simply `input.equals("hello")` — correct no matter how the String was built.

sections.title: == Checks the Address; .equals() Reads the Characters
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["s1 = hello (pooled literal)"] B["s2 = hello (pooled literal)"] C["s3 = new String(hello) (heap)"] A -->|"s1 == s2"| D["Same address → TRUE
both point to the pooled object"] A -->|"s1 == s3"| E["Different address → FALSE
s3 is a separate heap object"] A -->|"s1.equals(s3)"| F["Same characters → TRUE
both contain hello"] ``` Content can be identical; `==` is only `true` when the two variables are literally the same object.

sections.title: == vs .equals() for Strings
sections.content:
| | `==` | `.equals()` |
|---|---|---|
| Compares | Memory address (identity) | Characters (content) |
| Returns true when | Both variables point to exact same object | Both Strings contain same characters |
| Works for literals | Yes (by accident — pool sharing) | Yes |
| Works for `new String()` | No | Yes |
| Works for user input / API data | No | Yes |
| Null safe? | Yes (`null == null` is true) | No — throws NPE if called on null |
| Use for String content? | Never | Always |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `==` to compare String content** — it passes with literals because of the pool, then fails the instant the String comes from input, a file, an API, or `new String()`.
- **Calling `.equals()` on a possibly-null variable** — `name.equals("admin")` throws `NullPointerException` when `name` is `null`; flip it to `"admin".equals(name)` or use `Objects.equals()`.
- **Assuming `new String("hello") == "hello"` is `true`** — `new String(...)` always allocates a fresh heap object, so `==` is `false` even though the characters match.
- **Leaning on `intern()` to make `==` work** — interning forces pool membership, but code that depends on `==` for content is fragile; just call `.equals()`.

sections.title: When == Works by Accident — and When It Fails
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`==` compares references, not content** — two separate String objects with identical text return `false`.
- **`.equals()` compares characters** — returns `true` whenever the content matches, regardless of how each String was created.
- **`==` works for literals only by accident** — the String pool shares one object, so the bug hides until a String comes from input, a file, an API, or `new String()`.
- **Put the literal first for null-safety** — `"hello".equals(variable)` never throws; `variable.equals("hello")` throws `NullPointerException` if `variable` is `null`.
- **`Objects.equals(a, b)`** — the cleanest null-safe compare; handles both-null and one-null without an NPE.
- **`equalsIgnoreCase()`** — use it when case should not matter, instead of lowercasing both sides by hand.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Here is the thing candidates get burned by: `==` looks like it works for Strings, right up until it doesn't. It compares **references** — whether two variables point to the same object in memory — not the actual text. So it only returns `true` when both sides are literally the same object.

The reason it seems to work is the **String pool**. When you write two identical literals, Java hands you the same pooled object, so `==` happens to return `true`. But the moment a String comes from `scanner.nextLine()`, a REST response, a database read, or `new String("hello")`, you have a brand-new heap object — and `==` returns `false` even though the text is identical. That is the silent bug: it passes every quick test with literals and breaks in production with real input.

So my rule is simple — `.equals()` for any String content comparison, always. It walks the characters and does not care how the String was created.

Two things I would add to show I have actually hit this. First, null-safety: I write `"hello".equals(variable)` so a null variable cannot throw a `NullPointerException`, or I reach for `Objects.equals(a, b)` which handles nulls on both sides. And if case should not matter, `equalsIgnoreCase()` is cleaner than lowercasing by hand. Bottom line: `==` is identity, `.equals()` is content — and for Strings it is `.equals()` every time.

questions.question: What does String.compareTo() return and when do you use it?
questions.title: String.compareTo() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `compareTo()` returns an `int`: **0** if the strings are equal, a **negative number** if the calling string comes before the argument alphabetically, and a **positive number** if it comes after. It is used for lexicographic ordering — sorting strings, implementing `Comparable`, or any place that needs a three-way comparison.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the three-way return value semantics and know the difference between equals() (boolean) and compareTo() (ordering).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking compareTo() just returns -1, 0, or 1. It returns the actual character difference — 'b'.compareTo('a') returns 1, but 'hello'.compareTo('abc') returns 7 (difference in Unicode values of 'h' minus 'a').
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention compareToIgnoreCase() and that compareTo() is what you implement when a class implements Comparable<T> — it enables sorting via Collections.sort() and TreeMap keys.

sections.title: Not Just Equal or Not — Which One Comes First
sections.content:
At the plainest level, `compareTo()` compares two Strings alphabetically and tells you which one comes first. Where `.equals()` only answers *are these the same?* with a boolean, `compareTo()` answers *what is their order?* with an `int`.

That `int` has three cases:
- **`0`** — the two Strings are equal
- **a negative number** — the calling String comes **before** the argument
- **a positive number** — the calling String comes **after** the argument

How does it produce the number? It scans both Strings together and, at the first position where they differ, returns the difference between those two characters' Unicode values. So `"b".compareTo("a")` is `1` because `'b'` is `98` and `'a'` is `97`. If one String is a prefix of the other, it returns the difference in lengths.

The nuance: do not read meaning into the exact number — only its **sign** matters. `"hello".compareTo("abc")` returns `7`, not `1`, so always test `< 0`, `== 0`, or `> 0`.

The gotcha is **case**. Uppercase letters have smaller Unicode values than lowercase — `'A'` is `65`, `'a'` is `97` — so `"Apple".compareTo("apple")` is negative, and a naive sort puts every capitalised word ahead of lowercase ones. Use `compareToIgnoreCase()` when case should not drive the order. This is exactly the method you implement when your class implements `Comparable<T>`, which is what lets `Collections.sort()`, `Arrays.sort()`, and `TreeMap` keys order themselves.

sections.title: How compareTo() Turns Two Strings Into a Sign
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["s1.compareTo(s2)"] --> B{"First position
where they differ?"} B -->|"no difference"| C["returns 0
strings are equal"] B -->|"s1 char has smaller Unicode"| D["returns negative
s1 comes first"] B -->|"s1 char has larger Unicode"| E["returns positive
s1 comes after"] ``` The magnitude is the Unicode gap at that first differing character — but only the sign should ever drive your logic.

sections.title: compareTo() Return Value Meaning
sections.content:
| Return value | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | Strings are equal | `"apple".compareTo("apple")` → `0` |
| Negative | Calling string comes before argument | `"apple".compareTo("banana")` → negative |
| Positive | Calling string comes after argument | `"banana".compareTo("apple")` → positive |
| Check sign, not value | Exact number is char difference | `"b".compareTo("a")` → `1`, not always `-1` or `1` |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming it returns only `-1`, `0`, or `1`** — it returns the actual Unicode gap, so `"hello".compareTo("abc")` is `7`; branch on the sign, never on `== 1` or `== -1`.
- **Using `compareTo()` when you only need equality** — if the question is *are these the same?*, `equals()` is clearer and faster; reserve `compareTo()` for ordering.
- **Forgetting case ranks below lowercase** — `'A'` (65) sorts before `'a'` (97), so `"Zebra"` lands before `"apple"`; switch to `compareToIgnoreCase()` for human-friendly order.
- **Calling it on `null`** — `compareTo(null)` throws `NullPointerException`; guard first or order nulls explicitly with a `Comparator`.

sections.title: Using compareTo() for Sorting and Three-Way Comparison
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Returns an `int`, not a boolean** — `0` equal, negative = caller comes before, positive = caller comes after.
- **The number is the Unicode gap** at the first differing character — `"b".compareTo("a")` is `1`, `"hello".compareTo("abc")` is `7`; only the **sign** is contractual.
- **Uppercase sorts before lowercase** — `'A'` is `65`, `'a'` is `97`, so a raw sort puts `"Zebra"` ahead of `"apple"`; use `compareToIgnoreCase()`.
- **It powers sorting** — `Collections.sort()`, `Arrays.sort()`, `TreeMap`, and `TreeSet` all call `compareTo()` to order String keys.
- **It is the method behind `Comparable<T>`** — implement `compareTo()` in your own class to make it sortable, usually delegating to a field's `compareTo()`.
- **Branch on the sign** — write `if (s1.compareTo(s2) > 0)`, never `if (s1.compareTo(s2) == 1)`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The key shift from `equals()` is that `compareTo()` does not just tell you whether two Strings are the same — it tells you **their order**, which is what you need for sorting. It hands back an `int`: zero means equal, a negative number means the calling String comes first alphabetically, and a positive number means it comes after.

The detail people get wrong is assuming that number is always `-1`, `0`, or `1`. It is not — it is the difference in Unicode values at the first character where the two Strings diverge. So `"hello".compareTo("abc")` returns `7`, not `1`. The practical rule is to branch on the **sign** only — `< 0`, `== 0`, `> 0` — and never compare against a literal `1`.

The other thing I would flag is case. Uppercase letters have lower Unicode values than lowercase, so `"Apple"` sorts before `"apple"`, and a naive sort drops every capitalised word to the top. When case should not matter, `compareToIgnoreCase()` handles it.

Where this really earns its keep is `Comparable` — when you implement `compareTo()` on your own class, you usually delegate to a String field's `compareTo()`, and that is what lets `Collections.sort()`, `Arrays.sort()`, and `TreeMap` order your objects for free. So I think of `equals()` for yes/no and `compareTo()` for ranking — and I always check the sign, not the number.

What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
How does TreeMap use compareTo() to maintain sorted order?

questions.question: What are the common String search methods — contains(), startsWith(), endsWith()?
questions.title: String Search Methods: contains(), startsWith(), endsWith()
questions.direct_answer: `contains(s)` returns `true` if the substring `s` appears anywhere in the string. `startsWith(prefix)` checks if the string begins with the given prefix. `endsWith(suffix)` checks if it ends with the given suffix. All three return `boolean` and are case-sensitive.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the basic String search API and understand that all three are case-sensitive.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that these are all case-sensitive — 'Hello'.contains('hello') returns false.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention indexOf() returns the position (-1 if not found), which is useful when you need to know WHERE in the string something occurs, not just IF. Also mention that contains() is implemented using indexOf() internally.

sections.title: Three Yes/No Questions — Plus One That Tells You Where
sections.content:
At the plainest level, `contains()` tells you whether one String appears inside another. Java rounds this out with two siblings: `startsWith()` and `endsWith()`. All three return a plain `boolean`.

- `contains(s)` — is `s` anywhere inside this String?
- `startsWith(prefix)` — does this String begin with `prefix`?
- `endsWith(suffix)` — does this String end with `suffix`?

You reach for these constantly: checking a URL, validating a file extension with `name.endsWith(".pdf")`, or matching a command prefix.

How `contains()` actually works is worth knowing: it is implemented on top of `indexOf()`. `indexOf(s)` scans for the substring and returns the index where it starts, or `-1` if it is not there — and `contains()` simply returns whether that result is not `-1`. So they cost the same; the difference is what you get back: a position versus a yes/no.

The nuance: when you need to know **where** a match is — to slice the String, or find the next one with `lastIndexOf()` — call `indexOf()` directly instead of `contains()`.

The gotcha that bites everyone is **case sensitivity**. All of these compare exact characters, so `"Hello".contains("hello")` is `false`. There is no case-insensitive flag; the standard fix is to lowercase **both** sides first — `text.toLowerCase().contains(term.toLowerCase())` — which is the subject of the next question.

sections.title: Pick the Right Search Method for the Question
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["Searching inside a String"] --> B{"What do you need to know?"} B -->|"is it anywhere?"| C["contains(s)
returns boolean"] B -->|"at the start?"| D["startsWith(prefix)
returns boolean"] B -->|"at the end?"| E["endsWith(suffix)
returns boolean"] B -->|"where is it?"| F["indexOf(s)
returns index, or -1"] ``` All four are case-sensitive, and `contains()` is just `indexOf(s) != -1` under the hood.

sections.title: String Search Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
| Method | Returns | What it checks | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `contains(s)` | `boolean` | Is `s` anywhere in the string? | `"hello world".contains("world")` → `true` |
| `startsWith(prefix)` | `boolean` | Does the string begin with prefix? | `"https://".startsWith("https")` → `true` |
| `endsWith(suffix)` | `boolean` | Does the string end with suffix? | `"image.png".endsWith(".png")` → `true` |
| `indexOf(s)` | `int` | Position of first match, -1 if absent | `"hello".indexOf("ll")` → `2` |
| `lastIndexOf(s)` | `int` | Position of last match, -1 if absent | `"abcabc".lastIndexOf("a")` → `3` |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting they are case-sensitive** — `"Hello".contains("hello")` is `false`; normalise with `toLowerCase()` when case should not matter.
- **Normalising only one side** — `text.toLowerCase().contains(term)` still misses when `term` has capitals; lowercase **both** sides.
- **Using `contains()` when you need the position** — it only returns yes/no; reach for `indexOf()` when you have to slice or locate the match.
- **Treating `indexOf` returning `0` as not found** — `0` means the match is at the very start; only `-1` means absent.

sections.title: All Three Methods in Action
Key Points
sections.content:
- **All three are case-sensitive** — `"Hello".contains("hello")` is `false`; there is no case-insensitive overload.
- **`contains(s)`** checks anywhere, **`startsWith(p)`** checks the front, **`endsWith(s)`** checks the end — all return `boolean`.
- **`indexOf(s)`** returns the start position, or `-1` if absent — use it when you need *where*, not just *if*.
- **`contains()` is `indexOf(s) != -1`** internally — same cost, so choose based on whether you need the index.
- **`indexOf` returning `0`** means a match at the start, not "not found" — only `-1` means absent.
- **Case-insensitive search** needs `text.toLowerCase().contains(term.toLowerCase())` — normalise both sides.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
These are the three everyday substring checks, and they all hand back a simple boolean. `contains()` asks whether a substring appears anywhere; `startsWith()` checks the front; `endsWith()` checks the end — handy for things like `name.endsWith(".pdf")`.

The one mistake almost everyone makes is forgetting they are **case-sensitive**. `"Hello".contains("hello")` returns `false`, and there is no case-insensitive version built in. When case should not matter, I lowercase **both** sides — `text.toLowerCase().contains(term.toLowerCase())` — and the both part matters, because normalising only one side still misses.

The detail I would add to show I know the API is that `contains()` is really just `indexOf()` underneath: `indexOf(s)` returns the position of the first match, or `-1` if it is not there, and `contains()` simply checks whether that is not `-1`. So they cost the same. The practical takeaway is to pick based on what you need back — if I only want a yes/no, `contains()` reads cleanest; if I need to know *where* the match is so I can slice the String, I go straight to `indexOf()`.

What does String.matches() do and how is it different from contains()?

questions.question: How do you compare strings case-insensitively in Java?
questions.title: Case-Insensitive String Comparison in Java
questions.direct_answer: Use `String.equalsIgnoreCase(other)` to compare two Strings ignoring case. Use `compareToIgnoreCase(other)` for ordering. For `contains()`, `startsWith()`, and `endsWith()`, there is no built-in case-insensitive version — normalise both strings with `.toLowerCase()` first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know equalsIgnoreCase() and can explain the normalisation pattern for methods that lack a case-insensitive variant.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually comparing lowercased strings with == instead of .equals(). Or converting only one side to lowercase when using contains().
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that toLowerCase() and toUpperCase() should use Locale.ROOT in production to avoid the Turkish locale issue where 'i'.toUpperCase() produces 'İ' instead of 'I'.

sections.title: One Built-In for Equality — Normalise for Everything Else
sections.content:
At the plainest level, `equalsIgnoreCase()` compares two Strings for equality while ignoring upper- and lower-case differences, so `"Hello".equalsIgnoreCase("hello")` is `true`. Case-insensitive matching comes up everywhere — usernames, email addresses, file extensions, user-typed commands.

Why a dedicated method? Because the obvious do-it-yourself version is easy to get wrong, and `equalsIgnoreCase()` does the comparison without allocating new lowercased Strings.

For **ordering** there is a matching tool: `compareToIgnoreCase()`, which returns the same three-way `int` as `compareTo()` but ignores case.

Here is the nuance that surprises people: the **search** methods — `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `endsWith()` — have **no** case-insensitive variant. For those you normalise manually:

```java
url.toLowerCase().contains(term.toLowerCase()) // both sides lowered
```

The rule is to normalise **both** sides. Lowercasing only one side leaves the other's capitals in place, so a real match still slips through.

The production gotcha is **locale**. Plain `toLowerCase()` uses the JVM's default locale, and in the Turkish locale `'i'.toUpperCase()` becomes `'İ'` (a dotted capital I), not `'I'` — which silently breaks comparisons on a server set to that locale. For locale-independent normalisation in backend code, always pass `Locale.ROOT`: `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`.

sections.title: Built-In Where It Exists, Normalise Where It Doesn't
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["Compare ignoring case"] --> B{"What kind of comparison?"} B -->|"equality"| C["equalsIgnoreCase(other)
built-in"] B -->|"ordering"| D["compareToIgnoreCase(other)
built-in"] B -->|"contains / startsWith / endsWith"| E["no built-in
lowercase BOTH sides"] E --> F["use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)
to stay locale-safe"] ``` Equality and ordering have ready-made methods; search needs manual, two-sided normalisation.

sections.title: Case-Insensitive String Operations
sections.content:
| Operation | Method | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Equality check | `equalsIgnoreCase(other)` | Built-in — no normalisation needed |
| Ordering | `compareToIgnoreCase(other)` | Returns int like compareTo() |
| Contains substring | `s.toLowerCase().contains(t.toLowerCase())` | Normalise both sides |
| Starts with prefix | `s.toLowerCase().startsWith(p.toLowerCase())` | Normalise both sides |
| Ends with suffix | `s.toLowerCase().endsWith(suf.toLowerCase())` | Normalise both sides |
| Production safe | `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` | Avoids Turkish locale 'i' issue |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Lowercasing then comparing with `==`** — `a.toLowerCase() == b.toLowerCase()` compares references and is almost always `false`; use `equalsIgnoreCase()` or `.equals()`.
- **Normalising only one side for search** — `url.toLowerCase().contains(term)` misses when `term` has capitals; lowercase both sides.
- **Using default-locale `toLowerCase()` on a server** — the Turkish locale turns `'i'` into `'İ'`, breaking matches; pass `Locale.ROOT`.
- **Calling `equalsIgnoreCase()` on a `null` reference** — it still throws if the *caller* is null; put a known-non-null String first or guard the value.

sections.title: equalsIgnoreCase, compareToIgnoreCase, and the Normalise Pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`equalsIgnoreCase()`** is the clean built-in for case-insensitive equality — no lowercasing, no extra objects.
- **`compareToIgnoreCase()`** gives case-insensitive ordering with the same `int` semantics as `compareTo()`.
- **No built-in case-insensitive `contains()`/`startsWith()`/`endsWith()`** — normalise with `toLowerCase()` first.
- **Normalise both sides** — `s.toLowerCase().contains(t.toLowerCase())`; lowering only one side still mismatches.
- **Never lowercase-then-`==`** — that compares references; compare with `.equals()` or just use `equalsIgnoreCase()`.
- **Use `Locale.ROOT` in production** — default-locale `toLowerCase()` mangles `'i'` in the Turkish locale; `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` is locale-safe.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
For straight equality, I do not lowercase anything by hand — I use `equalsIgnoreCase()`. `"Hello".equalsIgnoreCase("hello")` is `true`, it handles every casing combination, and it does not allocate throwaway lowercased Strings. For ordering, `compareToIgnoreCase()` does the same job with the three-way `int` you get from `compareTo()`.

The trap is what people do when there is no built-in. The search methods — `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `endsWith()` — have no case-insensitive version, so you normalise yourself with `toLowerCase()` on **both** sides: `text.toLowerCase().contains(term.toLowerCase())`. Two things go wrong here. People lowercase only one side, so the other's capitals still cause a miss. And some lowercase both, then compare with `==` instead of `.equals()`, which compares references and fails — at that point you should have just called `equalsIgnoreCase()`.

The detail that separates a fresher from someone who has shipped server code is **locale**. Plain `toLowerCase()` uses the JVM's default locale, and in the Turkish locale a lowercase `'i'` does not round-trip to a plain `'I'` — it becomes a dotted capital, which silently breaks comparisons on a machine set to that locale. So in backend code I always pass `Locale.ROOT`: `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`. Built-in for equality and ordering, two-sided locale-safe normalisation for everything else.
